claim: E. coli faithfully segregates nucleoids across various growth rates despite lacking a ParABS system.
source: Yet, E. coli faithfully segregates nucleoids across various growth rates.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the introduction, establishing the biological context for the study.

claim: Polysome production during chromosomal gene expression helps compact, split, segregate, and position nucleoids in E. coli through nonequilibrium dynamics.
source: Here, we provide theoretical and experimental evidence that polysome production during chromosomal gene expression helps compact, split, segregate, and position nucleoids in E. coli through nonequilibrium dynamics that depend on polysome synthesis, degradation (through mRNA decay), and exclusion from the DNA meshwork.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by both theoretical modeling and experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Halting chromosomal gene expression and polysome production immediately stops sister nucleoid migration.
source: Halting chromosomal gene expression and thus polysome production immediately stops sister nucleoid migration, while ensuing polysome depletion gradually reverses nucleoid segregation.
evidence: This claim is supported by rifampicin treatment experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Polysome depletion gradually reverses nucleoid segregation.
source: Halting chromosomal gene expression and thus polysome production immediately stops sister nucleoid migration, while ensuing polysome depletion gradually reverses nucleoid segregation.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally with rifampicin treatment in Figure 6.

claim: Redirecting gene expression away from the chromosome and toward plasmids causes ectopic polysome accumulations that drive aberrant nucleoid dynamics.
source: Redirecting gene expression away from the chromosome and toward plasmids causes ectopic polysome accumulations that are sufficient to drive aberrant nucleoid dynamics.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 7 using plasmid-based mTagBFP2 overexpression.

claim: Cell width enlargement experiments suggest that limiting the exchange of polysomes across DNA-free regions ensures nucleoid segregation along the cell length.
source: Cell width enlargement experiments suggest that limiting the exchange of polysomes across DNA-free regions ensures nucleoid segregation along the cell length.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with A22 and cephalexin treatment shown in Figure 8.

claim: The mechanism couples nucleoid compaction and segregation to cell growth without the apparent requirement of regulatory molecules.
source: Our findings suggest a self-organizing mechanism for coupling nucleoid compaction and segregation to cell growth without the apparent requirement of regulatory molecules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined theoretical and experimental evidence presented in the study.

claim: Many bacterial species use a ParABS system to segregate a specific DNA region proximal to the chromosomal origin of replication.
source: Many bacterial species use a ParABS system to segregate a specific DNA region proximal to the chromosomal origin of replication (oriC) (Figge et al., 2003; Ireton et al., 1994; Jalal and Le, 2020; Lim et al., 2014; Livny et al., 2007; Mohl and Gober, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The ParABS system does not explain how the terminal regions of the chromosome separate or how sister nucleoids move away from each other.
source: However, this initial step does not explain how the terminal regions of the chromosome separate (Harju et al., 2024) or how sister nucleoids move away from each other.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the ParABS system, supported by citation.

claim: The chromosomally encoded parA and/or parB genes are often not essential for cell viability in various bacteria.
source: Moreover, the chromosomally encoded parA and/or parB genes are often not essential for cell viability in various bacteria (Bartosik et al., 2009; Charaka and Misra, 2012; Donczew et al., 2016; Donovan et al., 2010; Du et al., 2016; Ireton et al., 1994; Jakimowicz et al., 2007a; Jakimowicz et al., 2007b; Jecz et al., 2015; Kadoya et al., 2011; Kawalek et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2000; Lagage et al., 2016; Lee and Grossman, 2006; Lewis et al., 2002; Li, 2019; Li et al., 2015; Minnen et al., 2011; Santi and McKinney, 2015; Takacs et al., 2022; Yamaichi et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior research.

claim: Some bacteria do not encode a ParABS system for oriC partitioning, with E. coli being a prime example.
source: In fact, some bacteria do not even encode a ParABS system for oriC partitioning (Livny et al., 2007), with Escherichia coli being a prime example.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: DNA replication may facilitate chromosome partitioning through a DNA polymerase-dependent extrusion mechanism.
source: For example, DNA replication may facilitate chromosome partitioning through a DNA polymerase-dependent extrusion mechanism (Lemon and Grossman, 2000).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Simulations of coarse-grained polymer models have suggested that the conformational entropy of confined circular DNA chains could provide an unmixing force that separates two mixed DNA polymers.
source: Simulations of coarse-grained polymer models have also suggested that the conformational entropy of confined circular DNA chains could provide an unmixing force that separates two mixed DNA polymers (Jun and Mulder, 2006; Jun and Wright, 2010; Pande et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on prior modeling work, supported by citations.

claim: Recent modeling work has argued that entropic forces generated from excluded volume interactions between partially replicated chromosomes inhibit rather than promote their segregation.
source: However, recent modeling work has argued that entropic forces generated from excluded volume interactions between partially replicated chromosomes inhibit (rather than promote) their segregation (Harju et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on recent modeling work, supported by citation.

claim: E. coli mutants in which the mukB gene is deleted exhibit moderate nucleoid segregation defects linked to the organization and condensation of the nucleoid.
source: E. coli mutants in which the mukB gene required for DNA loop extrusion is deleted exhibit moderate nucleoid segregation defects linked to the organization and condensation of the nucleoid (Danilova et al., 2007; Mäkelä et al., 2021; Sawitzke and Austin, 2000).
evidence: This is based on prior experimental work, supported by citations.

claim: Most mukB deletion mutant cells successfully segregate and partition their nucleoids between daughter cells.
source: However, even in these mutants, most cells successfully segregate and partition their nucleoids between the daughter cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about mukB mutants, implying prior knowledge.

claim: Topoisomerase I mutations or seqA deletion suppress the chromosome segregation defects associated with mukB deletion.
source: Furthermore, topoisomerase I mutations or seqA deletion suppress the chromosome segregation defects associated with the mukB deletion (Danilova et al., 2007; Sawitzke and Austin, 2000; Weitao et al., 1999), suggesting that other mechanisms exist.
evidence: This is based on prior experimental work, supported by citations.

claim: In the presence of a poor-quality carbon source, E. coli initiates nucleoid segregation late in the cell division cycle.
source: In the presence of a poor-quality carbon source, E. coli initiates nucleoid segregation late in the cell division cycle.
evidence: This is stated as a known observation about E. coli growth.

claim: As the quality of the carbon source improves and the growth rate increases, nucleoid segregation occurs at an increasingly earlier stage of the cell division cycle.
source: As the quality of the carbon source improves and the growth rate increases, nucleoid segregation occurs at an increasingly earlier stage of the cell division cycle until it initiates in the preceding cycle to accommodate faster division times (Bates and Kleckner, 2005; Govers et al., 2024; Tiruvadi-Krishnan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Drug experiments have suggested that the chromosomal DNA is attached to the cytoplasmic membrane along the radial axis through a process known as transertion.
source: Drug experiments have indeed suggested that the chromosomal DNA is attached to the cytoplasmic membrane along the radial axis through a process known as transertion (Bakshi et al., 2015; Binenbaum et al., 1999; Kaval et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Matsumoto et al., 2015; Spahn et al., 2023; Woldringh, 2002), which occurs when transcription, translation, and insertion of membrane proteins occur at the same time.
evidence: This is based on prior experimental work, supported by citations.

claim: There is no evidence of localized growth of the cytoplasmic membrane between splitting nucleoids.
source: However, for the nucleoids to migrate directionally, the 1963 model requires localized growth of the cytoplasmic membrane between the splitting nucleoids. To our knowledge, there is no evidence of such localized expansion of the inner membrane.
evidence: This is stated as a lack of evidence for a specific mechanism.

claim: E. coli cells elongate via a dispersed mode of peptidoglycan growth along the cell length up to the final stage of the division cycle.
source: Even if the connection between the DNA and cytoplasmic membrane extends to the peptidoglycan cell wall, E. coli cells elongate via a dispersed mode of peptidoglycan growth along the cell length up to the final stage of the division cycle (Cooper and Hsieh, 1988; Navarro et al., 2022; Wientjes and Nanninga, 1989; Woldringh et al., 1987).
evidence: This is based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Experiments with B. subtilis cells stripped of their cell walls indicate that nucleoid segregation does not require cell wall attachment.
source: In addition, experiments with B. subtilis cells stripped of their cell walls indicate that nucleoid segregation does not require cell wall attachment (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on prior experimental work, supported by citation.

claim: The segregation of chromosomal loci is faster than the rate of cell elongation, ruling out cell elongation and nucleoid tethering to the membrane or cell wall as a major driver of chromosome segregation.
source: Finally, the segregation of chromosomal loci is faster than the rate of cell elongation, ruling out cell elongation and nucleoid tethering to the membrane or cell wall as a major driver of chromosome segregation (Kuwada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on prior experimental work, supported by citation.

claim: Experiments and modeling have suggested that macromolecular crowders exert compaction forces on the compressible nucleoids through steric (i.e. excluded-volume) interactions.
source: Experiments and modeling have suggested that macromolecular crowders exert compaction forces on the compressible nucleoids through steric (i.e. excluded-volume) interactions (Mondal et al., 2011; Pelletier et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2019a; Yang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The proteome fraction allocated to ribosomes increases with growth rate across nutrient conditions.
source: The proteome fraction allocated to ribosomes increases with growth rate across nutrient conditions (Chure and Cremer, 2023; Dai et al., 2016; Dourado and Lercher, 2020; Hu et al., 2020; Molenaar et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2014; Si et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The proportion of ribosomes engaged in translation increases with improving nutrient quality, attaining 70–80% under fast growth.
source: The proportion of ribosomes engaged in translation also increases with improving nutrient quality, attaining 70–80% under fast growth (Dai et al., 2016; Forchhammer and Lindahl, 1971; Mohapatra and Weisshaar, 2018; Sanamrad et al., 2014; Varricchio and Monier, 1971).
evidence: This is based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Polysomes form structures of comparable or larger size than the average ~50 nm mesh size of the nucleoid.
source: These polysomes form structures (Brandt et al., 2009) of comparable or larger size than the average ~50 nm mesh size of the nucleoid (Xiang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Fluorescently labeled ribosomes accumulate in DNA-free regions such as the cell poles and between segregated nucleoids.
source: Consistent with a steric clash between polysomes and the nucleoid meshwork, fluorescently labeled ribosomes accumulate in DNA-free regions such as the cell poles and between segregated nucleoids (Azam et al., 2000; Bakshi et al., 2015; Bakshi et al., 2012; Chai et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2019; Lewis et al., 2000; Mohapatra and Weisshaar, 2018; Robinow and Kellenberger, 1994; Sanamrad et al., 2014; Xiang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on prior experimental work, supported by citations.

claim: Theoretical work suggests that excluded-volume effects alone may be sufficient for the DNA to spontaneously phase separate from polysomes and compact into its observed nucleoid form.
source: Interestingly, theoretical work suggests that excluded-volume effects alone may be sufficient for the DNA to spontaneously phase separate from polysomes and compact into its observed nucleoid form (Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on prior theoretical work, supported by citation.

claim: A recent nonequilibrium statistical physics model proposes that nucleoid positioning and segregation could potentially be explained by the steric interaction between polysomes and DNA and the nonequilibrium effects associated with mRNA synthesis and degradation.
source: Furthermore, a recent nonequilibrium statistical physics model proposes that nucleoid positioning and segregation could potentially be explained by the steric interaction (i.e. repulsion) between polysomes and DNA and the nonequilibrium effects associated with mRNA synthesis and degradation (Miangolarra et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on prior theoretical work, supported by citation.

claim: In the theoretical model, polysome accumulation in the middle of the nucleoid emerges due to polysomes born in the middle of the nucleoid taking longer to diffuse out of the nucleoid than those born closer to the nucleoid edges.
source: In this theoretical model, polysome accumulation in the middle of the nucleoid emerges due to polysomes born in the middle of the nucleoid taking longer to diffuse out of the nucleoid than those born closer to the nucleoid edges.
evidence: This describes a mechanism from a prior theoretical model.

claim: Polysome accumulation beyond a certain concentration threshold drives phase separation between the DNA and polysomes at the mid-nucleoid location, resulting in nucleoid splitting.
source: Polysome accumulation beyond a certain concentration threshold drives phase separation between the DNA and polysomes at the mid-nucleoid location, resulting in nucleoid splitting.
evidence: This describes a mechanism from a prior theoretical model.

claim: The rate of polysome accumulation correlates with the rate of nucleoid segregation across cells.
source: The rate of polysome accumulation correlates with the rate of nucleoid segregation across cells
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1 with time-lapse microscopy data.

claim: CJW7323 cells were grown in M9gluCAAT in a microfluidic device.
source: CJW7323 cells were grown in M9gluCAAT in a microfluidic device.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1 and describes the experimental setup.

claim: The average relative timing of cell constriction initiation was estimated as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
source: The average relative timing of cell constriction initiation was estimated as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1C.

claim: Early during nucleoid migration (0–25% between the completion of nucleoid splitting and cell division), polysome accumulation contributes most to the measured variance in the displacement of the sister nucleoids.
source: The coefficients of the fitted mixed linear regressions suggest the following hypothesis: Early during nucleoid migration (0–25% between the completion of nucleoid splitting and cell division), polysome accumulation contributes most to the measured variance in the displacement of the sister nucleoids (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The contribution of polysome accumulation to nucleoid migration progressively decreases over time, while that of cell elongation increases.
source: This contribution progressively decreases over time, while that of cell elongation increases (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The polysome accumulation at mid-cell was reproducible across all conditions and strains, irrespective of the ribosomal subunit protein or the fluorescent tag used to mark ribosomes.
source: Demographs generated from these images revealed that the polysome accumulation at mid-cell was reproducible across all conditions and strains, irrespective of the ribosomal subunit protein (RplA or RpsB) or the fluorescent tag (msfGFP, mEos2, or GFP) used to mark ribosomes (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated with snapshot images across multiple strains and conditions in Figure 2.

claim: The richer the growth conditions, the earlier the polysome accumulation and the nucleoid splitting occurred in the division cycle based on relative cell lengths.
source: Importantly, and consistent with our prediction, the richer the growth conditions (i.e. the larger the average cell area), the earlier the polysome accumulation and the nucleoid splitting occurred in the division cycle based on relative cell lengths (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated with snapshot images across different nutrient conditions in Figure 2.

claim: There is a strong correlation (Spearman correlation ρ=–0.85) between the amplitude of the average ribosomal signal accumulation and the average nucleoid signal depletion at mid-cell.
source: We found a strong correlation (Spearman correlation ρ=–0.85) between the amplitude of the average ribosomal signal accumulation and the average nucleoid signal depletion at mid-cell (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B with quantitative correlation analysis across strains and nutrient conditions.

claim: Faster-growing populations displayed stronger polysome accumulation and greater DNA depletion at mid-cell on average.
source: Since the average cell area (colormap in Figure 2B) correlates with the growth rate of the population (Schaechter et al., 1958), this plot also confirmed that faster-growing populations displayed stronger polysome accumulation and greater DNA depletion at mid-cell on average (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B with data across different growth rates.

claim: Newborn cells had more polysomes at the new pole compared to the old one on average.
source: We found that newborn cells had more polysomes at the new pole compared to the old one on average (Figure 3A), consistent with the notion that polysomes do not rapidly equilibrate in concentration between DNA-free regions through diffusion.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with quantitative analysis of polysome distribution.

claim: The polysome distribution asymmetry between cell poles negatively correlated with the position of the nucleoid in newborn daughter cells.
source: Across cells, the polysome distribution asymmetry between cell poles negatively correlated with the position of the nucleoid in newborn daughter cells (Figure 3B, cells always oriented with the new pole to the right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with quantitative correlation analysis.

claim: The HupA-mCherry signal concentration was higher toward the new pole right after birth or, correspondingly, toward the middle of the cell (future new pole) in the period prior to division.
source: The average HupA-mCherry signal concentration was higher toward the new pole right after birth or, correspondingly, toward the middle of the cell (future new pole) in the period prior to division (Figure 3D and Video 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with 2D projections of fluorescence signals.

claim: The HupA-mCherry concentration is ~20% higher toward the new pole on average in newborn cells.
source: Quantification of this axial asymmetry in newborn cells revealed that the HupA-mCherry concentration is ~20% higher toward the new pole on average (Figure 3E), suggesting that the DNA density is uneven along the nucleoid length.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E with quantitative analysis.

claim: The relative availability of cell space depleted of polysomes correlated most strongly with the asymmetric distribution of DNA in newborn cells.
source: Compared to other polysome statistics, the relative availability of cell space depleted of polysomes (RplA-GFP signal) correlated most strongly with the asymmetric distribution of DNA (HupA-mCherry signal) in newborn cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F with quantitative correlation analysis.

claim: The model successfully captures the negative trend between the growth rate and the relative timing of nucleoid splitting.
source: We found that our model successfully captures the negative trend between the growth rate and the relative timing of nucleoid splitting. Simulated cells that grew faster also split their nucleoids earlier from birth to division, agreeing with population-level data (Figure 4D and Video 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D comparing model predictions to experimental data.

claim: The simulations reproduced the relatively constant cell length at which nucleoid splitting occurs across different growth rates.
source: The same simulations also reproduced the relatively constant cell length at which nucleoid splitting occurs across different growth rates (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), which was previously discovered in population-level measurements (Govers et al., 2024).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 comparing model predictions to experimental data.

claim: At diffusion coefficients below 0.005 μm2/s, the model reproduced the experimentally observed asymmetries, including the nucleoid position offset towards the new pole at birth, the higher polysome concentration at the new pole compared to the old one, and the asymmetric nucleoid compaction.
source: In fact, at diffusion coefficients below 0.005 μm2/s, the model (Figure 4E) reproduced the experimentally observed asymmetries, including the nucleoid position offset towards the new pole at birth, the higher polysome concentration at the new pole compared to the old one, and the asymmetric nucleoid compaction (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E comparing model predictions to experimental observations.

claim: In the shortest (i.e. newborn) cells, RplA-msfGFP-labeled polysomes had already accumulated within the nucleoid.
source: We found that in the shortest (i.e. newborn) cells, RplA-msfGFP-labeled polysomes had already accumulated within the nucleoid (Figure 5B, bin 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with 2D projections and particle density maps.

claim: mCherry-μNS particles were restricted to the cell poles and were not able to access the mid-cell region until after nucleoid splitting was clearly visible.
source: In contrast, mCherry-μNS particles were restricted to the cell poles and were not able to access the mid-cell region until after nucleoid splitting was clearly visible (Figure 5B, bins 2–4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with particle density maps across different cell length bins.

claim: Exposure to rifampicin led to the near-immediate arrest of nucleoid segregation.
source: Exposure to rifampicin led to the near-immediate arrest of nucleoid segregation (Figure 6B), consistent with our prediction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B with time-course data of nucleoid segregation during rifampicin treatment.

claim: The distance between the sister nucleoids remained the same for close to 30 min into rifampicin treatment, after which it started to decrease.
source: Interestingly, the distance between the sister nucleoids remained the same for close to 30 min into rifampicin treatment, after which it started to decrease (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B with time-course data during rifampicin treatment.

claim: About 30 min after rifampicin addition and further polysome depletion, the peak signals of the sister nucleoids started migrating closer to each other.
source: About 30 min after rifampicin addition and further polysome depletion, the peak signals of the sister nucleoids (white crosses, Figure 6C) started migrating closer to each other.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C with 1D and 2D fluorescence profiles during rifampicin treatment.

claim: After 1 hr of rifampicin treatment, when the RplA-GFP fluorescence was homogeneous, the two nucleoid objects fused into one.
source: Eventually, after 1 hr of rifampicin treatment, when the RplA-GFP fluorescence was homogeneous, the two nucleoid objects fused into one (Figure 6C), consistent with the dissipation of phase separation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C with fluorescence profiles during rifampicin treatment.

claim: Irrespective of their birth time (12 or 3 min before the addition of rifampicin), the negative correlation between polysome accumulation and nucleoid depletion at mid-cell was reversed ~9 min after the addition of the antibiotic, following the same path as for the untreated cells but in the opposite direction.
source: Irrespective of their birth time (12 or 3 min before the addition of rifampicin), the negative correlation between the two variables was reversed ~9 min after the addition of the antibiotic, following the same path as for the untreated cells but in the opposite direction (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D with correlation analysis during rifampicin treatment.

claim: Polysome depletion during rifampicin treatment resulted in correlated loss of asymmetric nucleoid compaction in newborn cells.
source: Polysome depletion during rifampicin treatment also resulted in correlated loss of asymmetric nucleoid compaction in newborn cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E with 1D and 2D fluorescence profiles.

claim: High expression of BFP2 from the plasmid slowed polysome production within the nucleoid and created polysome accumulations at ectopic cellular locations through the recruitment of ribosomes to plasmid transcripts.
source: We reasoned that high expression of BFP2 from the plasmid would slow polysome production within the nucleoid and create polysome accumulations at ectopic cellular locations through the recruitment of ribosomes to plasmid transcripts.
evidence: This is the experimental design rationale for the plasmid overexpression experiment.

claim: The gradual increase of mTagBFP2 fluorescence in the cells was associated with a concomitant decrease in cell growth rate.
source: The gradual increase of mTagBFP2 fluorescence in the cells was associated with a concomitant decrease in cell growth rate (Figure 7C), consistent with reduced gene expression from the chromosome.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with time-course data of growth rate during induction.

claim: IPTG-induced cells displayed a similar scaling relationship between the intensity of DNA (labeled with DRAQ5) and cell size (side scatter area) to uninduced cells.
source: We verified by flow cytometry that induction did not block DNA replication. IPTG-induced cells displayed a similar scaling relationship between the intensity of DNA (labeled with DRAQ5) and cell size (side scatter area) to uninduced cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 with flow cytometry data.

claim: Induced cells displayed various patterns of polysome accumulations, presumably due to stochastic clustering of plasmids in DNA-free regions.
source: We found that induced cells displayed various patterns of polysome accumulations (Video 5), presumably due to stochastic clustering of plasmids in DNA-free regions as previously reported for multi-copy plasmids devoid of DNA partitioning genes (Hsu and Chang, 2019; Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is shown in Video 5 and supported by citations to prior research on plasmid clustering.

claim: In some cells, polysomes accumulated at one pole instead of the middle of the nucleoid, preventing the nucleoid from splitting.
source: Importantly, the ectopic accumulations of polysomes had a drastic effect on nucleoid dynamics. In some cells, polysomes accumulated at one pole instead of the middle of the nucleoid, preventing the nucleoid from splitting (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D with time-lapse images of cells during induction.

claim: In other cells, polysome accumulation occurred between sister nucleoids, but did not relocate to the segregated nucleoids at the ¼ and ¾ cell positions.
source: In other cells, polysome accumulation occurred between sister nucleoids, but did not relocate to the segregated nucleoids at the ¼ and ¾ cell positions. Rather, polysome accumulation persisted and expanded between the sister nucleoids, effectively further pushing them apart (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E with time-lapse images of cells during induction.

claim: Both phenotypes (polar polysome accumulation and inter-nucleoid polysome accumulation) were reproduced by the model when an accumulation of polysomes was intentionally caused, either at a pole or between segregated nucleoids.
source: Both of these phenotypes were reproduced by our model when we intentionally caused an accumulation of polysomes, either at a pole or between segregated nucleoids (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 with model simulations.

claim: Cell width enlargement led to cells with a polysome phase at the cell center surrounded by a nucleoid phase around the cell periphery.
source: To test these ideas, we first treated cultures with A22 to inhibit cell width control through the inactivation of MreB (Bean et al., 2009; Iwai et al., 2002). This resulted in cells with a polysome phase at the cell center surrounded by a nucleoid phase around the cell periphery (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, top).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 with images of A22-treated cells.

claim: Cephalexin treatment alone resulted in filamentous cells (of constant cell width) with multiple nucleoids separated by polysome accumulations.
source: As a control, we showed that cephalexin treatment alone resulted in filamentous cells (of constant cell width) with multiple nucleoids separated by polysome accumulations (Figure 8B), consistent with previous reports (Chai et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2019; Thappeta et al., 2024).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B with images of cephalexin-treated cells and supported by citations.

claim: In cells treated with both A22 and cephalexin, drug treatment resulted in a single large polysome accumulation at the cell center, with the nucleoid displaying a toroidal shape at the cell periphery.
source: In cells treated with both drugs, we observed two types of subcellular rearrangements. In smaller cells, which started with a single nucleoid, drug treatment resulted in a single large polysome accumulation at the cell center, with the nucleoid displaying a toroidal shape at the cell periphery (Figure 8C and Video 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C with images of A22+cephalexin-treated cells.

claim: In longer cells with two segregated nucleoids treated with A22 and cephalexin, the nucleoids expanded and were often aberrantly segregated along the cell width concomitant with polysome accumulation at the site of nucleoid splitting.
source: In longer cells with two segregated nucleoids, the nucleoids expanded and were often aberrantly segregated along the cell width concomitant with polysome accumulation at the site of nucleoid splitting (white arrowheads, Figure 8D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D with images of A22+cephalexin-treated cells.

claim: Cell width enlargement led to the coalescence of polysome accumulations toward the cell center and the fusion of nucleoids around the cell periphery.
source: Cell width enlargement led to the coalescence of polysome accumulations toward the cell center and the fusion of nucleoids around the cell periphery (Figure 8C–E, Figure 8—figure supplement 1, bottom).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 8C-E with images of A22+cephalexin-treated cells.

claim: The nucleoids and polysome accumulations decreased in number while increasing in size in cephalexin/A22-treated cells compared to cephalexin-treated cells with the same cell area distribution but normal cell width.
source: As a result, the nucleoids and polysome accumulations decreased in number while increasing in size in cephalexin/A22-treated cells compared to cephalexin-treated cells with the same cell area distribution but normal cell width (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8F with quantitative comparison between treatments.

claim: An appealing feature of this proposed model is that polysomes inherently integrate the rate of nucleoid segregation with that of gene expression and cell growth.
source: An appealing feature of this proposed model is that polysomes inherently integrate the rate of nucleoid segregation with that of gene expression and cell growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined evidence presented in the study.

claim: The concentration of polysomes and their rate of accumulation in the cell directly reflect the transcriptional and translational activities in the cell.
source: The concentration of polysomes and their rate of accumulation in the cell directly reflect the transcriptional and translational activities in the cell (Balakrishnan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the proposed model, an increase in polysome concentration not only leads to more protein synthesis and faster cell growth but also results in faster nucleoid segregation.
source: Thus, in our proposed model, an increase in polysome concentration not only leads to more protein synthesis and faster cell growth but also results in faster nucleoid segregation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model and experimental evidence.

claim: The rod-shaped cell morphology ensures that the nucleoid grows exclusively along one dimension, the cell length.
source: The rod-shaped cell morphology ensures that the nucleoid grows exclusively along one dimension, the cell length.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of cell geometry.

claim: The nucleoid attachment to the membrane along the radial cell axis, through transertion, may act as a diffusion barrier and limit polysome exchange between distinct DNA-free regions.
source: Furthermore, the nucleoid attachment to the membrane along this radial cell axis, through transertion, may act as a diffusion barrier and limit polysome exchange between distinct DNA-free regions.
evidence: This is proposed as a mechanism based on the experimental observations.

claim: Control of cell width appears vital to uphold the constraint that nucleoid grows along a single-cell axis and promote that nucleoid segregation.
source: Control of cell width appears vital to uphold this constraint and promote that nucleoid grows along a single-cell axis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell width enlargement experiments.

claim: This explains the drastic improvement in nucleoid segregation of wall-less cells (L-forms) when compressed to normal width.
source: This explains the drastic improvement in nucleoid segregation of wall-less cells (L-forms) when compressed to normal width (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior research in light of the current findings.

claim: Nucleoid segregation may have imposed an evolutionary constraint on cell width control.
source: It highlights the importance of cell width regulation and suggests that nucleoid segregation may have imposed an evolutionary constraint on cell width control.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the findings.
